title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Shared radix-4 combinational divider with parallel trial subtraction
motivation:
The baseline has a 199.837 ns, 156-cell worst path through forwarding,
the execute-stage ALU, and the result register, and reaches only 5.442 MHz.
The ALU expresses signed and unsigned quotient and remainder with four
separate / and % operators. Deep combinational division is the strongest
candidate for this path. Reducing its serial logic depth should raise
CoreMark iterations/second without adding instruction cycles or changing
the existing memory-stall behavior. No earlier micro_opt attempts or
distilled lessons exist for this fixture beyond the baseline retest.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace only the real DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU arithmetic in alu.sv with one
shared, fully combinational unsigned radix-4 quotient/remainder network.
Normalize signed DIV/REM operands to 32-bit unsigned magnitudes; unsigned
operations use the original operands. Consume the dividend two bits at
a time, most significant pair first, in sixteen unrolled stages. Starting
with remainder R=0, each stage forms the 34-bit trial T={R,next_pair}.
Precompute zero-extended D, 2D, and 3D once with enough width to prevent
overflow. Compute T-D, T-2D, and T-3D in parallel as 35-bit unsigned
subtractions. Their borrow bits select the largest nonnegative candidate
and the corresponding quotient digit 1, 2, or 3; select T and digit 0
when all three borrow. Use mutually exclusive digit predicates and a
parallel masked-OR remainder mux rather than a cascaded priority data
mux. For nonzero D, every selected remainder is less than D and fits
32 bits. Concatenate the sixteen two-bit digits to obtain the quotient,
and use the final remainder directly, avoiding q*D remainder recovery.
Restore the quotient sign using the dividend/divisor sign XOR and the
remainder sign using the dividend sign. Explicit final overrides retain
division-by-zero and INT_MIN/-1 quotient/remainder semantics. Keep the
module interface, zero-cycle combinational ALU latency, all nondivision
operations, and the exact RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS substitutions unchanged.
This is one local arithmetic-implementation optimization: it replaces
up to 32 dependent radix-2 decisions with 16 parallel-trial radix-4
decisions, while sharing signed/unsigned quotient/remainder hardware.
The prediction is a meaningful median Gowin Fmax improvement at unchanged
CoreMark cycles; routing cost from three subtractors per stage is the
principal risk and must be assessed by the existing FPGA evaluation.
An independent fixed-width software model of the 35-bit borrow tests,
exclusive digit predicates, recurrence, sign restoration, and exceptions
matched integer-reference results for 201174 signed/unsigned operand
pairs, including deterministic random and directed boundary cases.
RTL correctness and the predicted timing gain remain to be evaluated.

title: Remove unrolled division from EX with a blocking iterative divider
motivation:
The baseline scores 12.12 CoreMark iterations/second at only 5.442 MHz.
Its worst vendor timing path is 199.837 ns across 156 cells, traversing
forwarding and u_ex/u_alu. The ALU implements signed and unsigned DIV
and REM with combinational / and % operators, exposing a full unrolled
division network to timing even when CoreMark executes ordinary integer
instructions. Replacing this network with registered iterative execution
should greatly improve Fmax and reduce LUT pressure. Source inspection
finds division/remainder expressions in list/matrix initialization and
main setup/reporting, while the timed list, matrix and state kernels
contain none. Thus divider latency is expected to have little impact on
bracketed cycles; dynamic instruction counts remain to be verified.
The local history contains only the baseline retest and no prior
structural attempts; LESSONS.md is absent.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make DIV, DIVU, REM and REMU blocking multicycle EX operations using one
shared radix-2 restoring divider. Capture the post-forwarding operands
and operation exactly once, register quotient/remainder state, and
perform one 33-bit subtract/select step per cycle for 32 iterations.
Register sign correction and the final result before it returns to the
ordinary EX/MEM path. This removes every real combinational / and %
operator from the synthesized ALU, while keeping RV32I and multiplication
at their current latency.

Freeze fetch and ID/EX while the divider owns EX, but let older EX/MEM
and MEM/WB instructions drain. Insert invalid, side-effect-free EX/MEM
bubbles while waiting; do not repeatedly hold and reissue an older
memory operation. Existing dmem backpressure still holds a pending older
memory request, and has priority over advancing EX/MEM. Accept a divide
only from a valid legal instruction when EX can start it; retain a
completed result until downstream accepts it. On that acceptance edge,
release ID/EX and transfer the captured instruction and operands with
its result exactly once. Captured operands must not depend on forwarding
sources remaining live after older instructions retire. Qualify redirects
with a valid instruction actually advancing, and cancel divider state on
reset. Preserve the nret=1 interface, channel-0 retirement order and all
existing decoder, trap, memory and RVFI behavior.

Implement signed division by unsigned magnitudes, restoring quotient sign
from the operand-sign XOR and remainder sign from the dividend. Preserve
truncation toward zero, quotient all-ones/remainder dividend on division
by zero, and INT_MIN/-1 quotient INT_MIN/remainder zero. Keep all existing
RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS formulas bit-identical; pass their registered results
through the same request/completion handshake within the existing formal
depth, using the established arithmetic abstraction rather than changing
any formal configuration. Real-arithmetic unit tests and cosim must check
full divider latency, corners and handshake behavior.

Fitness improves if the Fmax ratio exceeds the CoreMark cycle-count ratio
by more than 1.046. Relative to 4,491,485 baseline bracketed cycles, use
the actual increase in cycles and the measured vendor median Fmax to test
this tradeoff. A several-fold clock improvement is plausible after removing
the 32-step combinational division chain; remaining multiplication or
forwarding paths and dynamic divide frequency are the principal risks.

title: 64-entry tagged next-PC predictor with two-bit branch direction
motivation:
The baseline fetches sequentially and flushes the combinational IF/ID
instruction whenever EX resolves a taken branch or jump. Because IF/ID
is not registered, each such transfer loses one fetch/decode opportunity,
rather than the two bubbles suggested by the five-stage comments.
CoreMark repeatedly executes loop branches and call sites, making these
bubbles a promising source of cycle savings. The measured 199.837 ns
critical path is through forwarding and the combinational ALU; a small
PC-indexed predictor should improve iterations/cycle without adding
logic to that arithmetic path. No predictor experiments or lessons are
present in this fixture's history.

A fresh architectural trace of the canonical -O3, RV32IM, 2K,
ten-iteration CoreMark ELF contains 2,922,016 bracketed instructions,
529,588 conditional branches, 49,367 JALs, and 13,735 JALRs. Sequential
prediction would mispredict 357,527 next PCs. A 64-entry tagged table
with this policy reduces next-PC errors to 62,551; 32 entries give
73,619 errors and 128 entries give 58,167. Thus 64 entries capture most
of the available benefit without doubling storage for only 4,384 fewer
errors. This trace model uses immediate training and no speculative
pipeline or bus timing, so it supports the sizing decision rather than
constituting a measured RTL speedup.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one 64-entry direct-mapped tagged branch-target buffer in if_stage.
Index with fetch PC[7:2]; each entry holds a valid bit, PC[31:8] tag,
aligned 30-bit target, unconditional-transfer bit, and a two-bit
saturating conditional-branch counter. Reset valid bits only, keeping
payload arrays free of reset to permit distributed-memory inference.
A matching unconditional entry or conditional counter with its high bit
set predicts the stored target; a miss predicts PC+4. Use only the
registered fetch PC for lookup, avoiding an imemData-to-next-PC decode
or immediate-adder path. Preserve the combinational IF/ID topology.

Carry the exact predicted_next_pc used for an accepted fetch through
IF/ID and ID/EX. EX still resolves all control transfers using forwarded
operands and retains the existing target-alignment checks. Compute the
architectural next PC for every valid instruction, including PC+4 for
ordinary instructions and the existing trap fall-through behavior.
Redirect and flush the younger instruction only when this resolved next
PC differs from the captured predicted_next_pc. Comparing every valid
instruction also repairs a stale BTB prediction if code at a trained PC
changes to a non-control or illegal instruction. Correctly predicted
taken transfers must advance with no recovery bubble; JAL/JALR still
write PC+4 and RVFI reports the resolved architectural next PC.

Train exactly once when a valid instruction advances out of EX, never
while EX/MEM is held by a dmem stall. Allocate only legal aligned
control transfers; initialize a new conditional entry to weakly taken
or weakly not-taken according to its outcome and saturate on subsequent
matching resolutions. Branch entries store PC+imm even on not-taken
outcomes; JAL/JALR entries store the resolved target and predict taken
unconditionally. Invalidate a matching stale entry on non-control,
illegal, or misaligned resolution. Lookup during a simultaneous update
uses the pre-edge entry, and the captured prediction remains the
authoritative recovery metadata regardless of subsequent table changes.

A normal predicted PC update occurs only when fetch/decode accepts the
instruction: imemReady, no load-use stall, no dmem hold, and no recovery
flush. Recovery is gated by valid EX advancement, overrides an imem
stall, and selects the resolved PC ahead of prediction. During a dmem
hold, retain the pending instruction and its prediction until it can
resolve and advance; do not repeatedly train or redirect it. Preserve
all bus handshake semantics, decoder validation, memory side-effect
gating, and the existing nret=1 RVFI port and retirement-order contract.

Saving all 294,976 redirects suggested by the architectural trace would
give about 7.0 percent fitness gain against the recorded 4,491,485
cycles at unchanged Fmax. Allowing for overlap with imem stalls, expect
approximately 6 percent; this is a hypothesis, not a measured result.
Predictor collisions, irregular directions, changing JALR targets,
update timing, and Gowin mapping can reduce the gain. Validate with
existing formal and cosim gates, canonical CoreMark CRCs under both bus
stalls, and vendor median timing; acceptance requires over 4.6 percent
fitness improvement. Do not change arithmetic, pipeline depth, or eval
files.

title: Remove redirect fanout from decode and register-file reads
motivation:
The champion's blocking iterative divider improved fitness to 110.00
at a median 49.408 MHz with 4,491,817 bracketed CoreMark cycles. Its
reported worst vendor path is now 26.211 ns across 36 cells through
u_id, u_ex, u_if, u_hazard and back to u_id. In the current RTL, EX
redirect replaces the entire combinational IF/ID instruction with a
NOP before decoding, register-file address selection and load-use
comparison. Redirect also clears the complete wide ID/EX payload.
These late control dependencies are candidates for unnecessary path
depth and fanout. LESSONS.md establishes that the accepted iterative
divider must be retained; the prior micro_opt trial only optimized
unrolled division and did not address this new critical path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Apply one local control-path optimization: represent killed fetches
and pipeline bubbles through validity and side-effect controls, while
removing redirect-dependent muxes from instruction and operand data.
Preserve the current pipeline topology, instruction latencies, divider,
fetch PC update policy and memory handshake behavior.

In if_stage, pass imem_data directly to out.instr even on a flush or
redirect. Retain the existing out.valid qualification and the existing
priority of reset, redirect and fetch hold for updating the PC. Invalid
instruction payloads are internal don't-care data, never retirements.
In id_stage, clock the wide instruction, PC, immediate, source-address,
destination-address and operand payload whenever the existing stall
permits, independently of flush. Separately update control and valid:
reset clears state; flush clears valid and the entire ctrl_t; an
unstalled invalid input also captures valid=0 and ctrl_t='0; a valid
accepted input captures the complete validated decoder output. A hold
retains the pending valid instruction and all its data. In particular,
load-use still injects its bubble even though stall is asserted, and
dmem/divider holds retain their existing precedence over that bubble.
Clearing only valid would be insufficient because existing forwarding
and memory request logic consume control bits without valid gating.

Compute load-use comparisons from the raw fetch instruction fields,
qualified by imem_ready and a valid ID/EX load with nonzero rd. Do not
qualify this data-path stall with redirect-derived IF/ID validity: doing
so would restore the same late redirect-to-operand-register dependency.
A redirecting EX instruction cannot simultaneously be a valid load.
Preserve all existing stall/flush equations and their priorities apart
from this equivalent qualification, including clearing MEM/WB valid
while retaining forwarding data during dmem backpressure. Wire any
added ID/EX-valid input internally without changing core's ports.

This should remove redirect-to-instruction-decode/register-file-address
paths and redirect-driven clearing of wide ID/EX data, leaving redirect
to affect only PC recovery and narrow validity/control state. Predict
unchanged bracketed CoreMark cycles and a 15 percent fitness improvement
from higher Fmax. The timing prediction is unmeasured; remaining branch,
register-file, multiply and bus-stall paths can limit the gain. Accept
only if measured median Gowin Fmax times actual iterations/cycle exceeds
110.00 by more than 4.6 percent (fitness greater than 115.06).

Existing decoder legality, misalignment handling, RV32M arithmetic,
nret=1 RVFI ordering and all correctness gates remain mandatory. Verify
no wrong-path store, register write, divider start or redirect occurs
when raw invalid instruction data encodes a side-effecting operation.
Exercise recovery coincident with imem stalls, prolonged dmem holds,
load-use hazards and divider ownership. Use unchanged formal/cosim and
canonical stalled CoreMark CRC checks, plus vendor timing, to evaluate
correctness and the proposed path reduction.

title: Register the fetch/decode boundary to break EX redirect feedback
motivation:
The champion's blocking iterative divider removed the dominant arithmetic
chain and raised median Gowin Fmax to 49.408 MHz at 4,491,817 bracketed
CoreMark cycles, scoring 110.00 iterations/second. Its remaining reported
worst path is 26.211 ns across 36 cells through u_id, u_ex, u_if,
u_hazard and back into u_id. The current IF/ID bundle is combinational:
EX redirect forces the instruction bus to a NOP, which changes decode,
register-file read addresses and load-use detection in the same cycle.
A real register boundary between fetch and decode should remove this
long control-to-data feedback path. The structural history contains only
the successful iterative-divider change; retain that established lesson.

Add one elastic, registered IF/ID entry containing PC, instruction and
valid, making fetch and decode separate stages. Decode, immediate
generation and register-file addresses must depend only on this stored
entry, never on live imemData or an EX-redirect-selected NOP. Continue
issuing at most one instruction per cycle with the unchanged nret=1
top-level interface. Keep the existing iterative DIV/REM implementation,
ordinary execution units, memory protocol and architectural behavior.

Treat entry consumption and fetch acceptance separately. Decode may
consume a valid buffered instruction whenever ID/EX can accept it even
if imemReady is low. Fetch may capture imemData when imemReady is high
and the entry is empty or is being consumed that cycle; simultaneous
consume/refill sustains one instruction per cycle. Advance the fetch PC
only on a captured fetch. While decode is blocked by load-use, dmem
backpressure or divider ownership, preserve an occupied entry and its
PC; an empty entry may capture one instruction and then stop fetching.
Do not overwrite an unconsumed entry or execute a fetch twice.

An aligned taken transfer resolving in an advancing EX instruction
redirects the fetch PC with priority over bus stalls and invalidates
both the younger buffered instruction and the younger ID/EX instruction.
Reject simultaneous refill on this recovery edge. Recovery must clear
validity without selecting a NOP onto the instruction/decode/regfile
address buses or synchronously clearing all payload bits on recovery.
Retain payload on flush and initialize buffer validity on reset; preserve
deterministic reset values for existing pipeline payloads, architectural
registers and divider state. This costs one extra recovery cycle compared with
the current combinational IF/ID design, but removes the serial EX-to-
instruction-mux-to-decode-to-register-read path.

Make every invalid pipeline token side-effect-free. Gate memory requests,
register writes, divider starts and redirects with the owning valid bit;
invalidate EX/MEM forwarding on bubbles. Load-use detection examines the
registered IF/ID instruction and a valid ID/EX load, injecting an ID/EX
bubble while retaining the buffered consumer. Preserve the existing
MEM/WB data-retention forwarding behavior during dmem holds, and ensure
an invalid token cannot replace that retained forwarding data with a
falsely live destination. Older memory operations still hold stable
address/data/masks until accepted and drain exactly once. Divider waits
retain ID/EX and its captured operation while older stages drain. Only
a valid advancing EX transfer can recover the frontend, so dmem stalls
cannot lose or repeatedly apply a redirect. Retire valid instructions
in order on channel 0 with contiguous RVFI order and correct operands.

Prior CoreMark architectural tracing reports 357,527 taken transfers
among 2,922,016 bracketed instructions. Charging one extra cycle per
transfer gives a first-order budget of about 4,849,344 cycles, 8 percent
above the champion; bus-stall overlap and the one-entry buffer alter
that estimate and must be measured. With that cycle count, acceptance
requires median Fmax above approximately 55.8 MHz, since the Fmax ratio
divided by the measured cycle-count ratio must exceed 1.046. A 65 MHz
clock would yield roughly 22 percent fitness gain under this estimate.
Predict 20 percent with medium confidence: the removed feedback is the
observed worst path, but remaining multiplier, divider-step, register-
file and PC-update paths may become limiting. Validate actual cycle
count, canonical CRCs and vendor median timing; this is an unmeasured
architectural hypothesis, not a claim of achieved improvement.

title: PC-indexed next-PC prediction with a short recovery control path
motivation:
The current champion already removes combinational DIV/REM from EX and
reaches fitness 110.00 at 49.408 MHz. Preserve that implementation. The
earlier 64-entry predictor experiment reduced bracketed CoreMark cycles
from 4,491,485 to 4,197,517, but its 5.487 MHz result still contained the
original combinational divider; it does not measure predictor timing on
the current champion. This is direct evidence for useful prediction,
rather than evidence that a predictor should replace the divider fix.

The champion's reported worst path is 26.211 ns through register-file
data, ID, EX, IF, hazard logic, and ID again. Currently an EX redirect
masks all 32 instruction bits to NOP before decode and load-use checks,
even though a recovery only needs to invalidate the younger instruction.
Because IF/ID is combinational, a taken control transfer costs one fetch
opportunity. A PC-only predictor can eliminate most of these bubbles,
provided its recovery does not deepen that existing control path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one 64-entry direct-mapped tagged next-PC predictor, using the current
iterative-divider champion as the starting point. Index by PC[7:2] and
store a full PC[31:8] tag, aligned target[31:2], valid bit, unconditional
flag, and two-bit saturating conditional direction counter. Lookup uses
only the registered fetch PC, never instruction-memory data, EX operands,
or a same-cycle update bypass. A hit predicts the target for unconditional
transfers or a taken counter; otherwise predict PC+4. Reset valid bits
only and leave payload arrays without reset to permit LUT-RAM inference.
Keep the current combinational IF/ID topology and single retirement port.

Carry the exact predicted next PC with each accepted instruction into
ID/EX. EX continues to resolve branches using forwarded operands, checks
target alignment, and produces the architectural pc_next independently
of prediction. Compare the captured prediction with both PC+4 and the
resolved control target in parallel, then select the mismatch using the
resolved branch/jump outcome. Do not first select a 32-bit architectural
next PC and then put a wide equality comparator behind that mux. Check
every valid instruction so a stale prediction for ordinary or illegal
code also recovers to the existing architectural fall-through PC.
Correct predictions cause no flush; mispredictions recover to resolved
pc_next with priority over imemReady and fetch stalls. Jumps still write
PC+4 and RVFI always reports the resolved architectural successor.

Integrate recovery by keeping the instruction and decoded data paths
independent of redirect. Remove redirect/flush-dependent 32-bit NOP
selection in IF. Use a narrow valid/kill path in ID instead: an accepted
invalid fetch or recovery injects a bubble with side-effect controls,
including reg_write, mem_read, mem_write, and control-transfer flags,
cleared. Only reset clears the wide ID/EX payload. Instruction, operand,
PC, and prediction data registers use stall enables independent of
recovery; their contents are irrelevant when valid and side effects are
cleared. Hazard inputs use raw instruction source fields and imemReady
as fetch availability, independently of redirect. Do not use a fetch
validity signal already masked by redirect to drive load-use detection
or wide data-register enables. Recovery takes precedence for PC update
and validity killing. Dmem and divider holds retain their existing
priority and forwarding behavior. Invalid payloads must not create
forwarding writers, memory requests, division requests, or retirement.
Do not change stage depth, arithmetic, register-file storage, or buses.

Train once per valid instruction advancing from EX, gated by !reset,
!stall_ex_mem, and !ex_wait. Allocate legal aligned branches and jumps
only. Branches store PC+imm even when not taken; new counters start weak
in the resolved direction, while matching counters saturate. JAL/JALR
store the resolved aligned target and predict unconditionally. Invalidate
a matching entry on ordinary, illegal, or misaligned resolution. Retain
original prediction metadata through load-use, dmem, and divider holds;
never train or redirect repeatedly while EX is held. Lookup observes the
pre-edge table on concurrent training. Fetch advances on prediction only
when imemReady is high and ID accepts the instruction without recovery.

At unchanged Fmax, repeating the previous measured cycle reduction on
4,491,817 champion cycles would improve fitness by about 7 percent, above
the 4.6 percent acceptance threshold. The narrow recovery path is intended
to preserve Fmax despite the added mismatch test; timing improvement is
not assumed in the estimate. Validate canonical CoreMark CRCs and marker
cycles under both bus stalls, existing formal/cosim gates, and Gowin
median Fmax. At the previous predictor cycle count, median Fmax must be
above approximately 48.30 MHz to exceed fitness 115.06, the champion's
4.6 percent acceptance threshold. Predictor lookup and recovery timing
are the principal risks; the old divider-limited timing cannot establish
whether this margin survives on the champion.

title: Shared signedness-selectable multiplier fed directly by forwarded registers
motivation:
The champion scores 119.03 at 49.962 MHz and 4,197,447 bracketed
CoreMark cycles. LESSONS.md identifies the remaining register-file,
forwarding and DSP-multiply path after redirect optimization; round-2
micro_opt and structural attempts left this limit in place. The ALU
currently infers three separate signed/unsigned full-width products
(six DSP resources), all fed through AUIPC/immediate operand muxes even
though every RV32M multiply is a register-register instruction.
Reproducing the champion at placement option 0 yielded exactly the
logged 49.053 MHz and 25.681 ns worst arrival, establishing a comparable
vendor timing baseline. The earlier micro_opt divider proposal retained
an unrolled divide path; the champion has already removed that limit.

The champion scores 119.03 at 49.962 MHz and 4,197,447 bracketed
CoreMark cycles. LESSONS.md identifies the remaining register-file,
forwarding and DSP-multiply path after redirect optimization; round-2

(six DSP resources), all fed through AUIPC/immediate operand muxes even
though every RV32M multiply is a register-register instruction.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Optimize only the combinational multiplier operand/result datapath.
Use one shared signed 33-by-33-bit multiplication, fed directly by the
existing post-forwarding rs1 and rs2 buses, bypassing the AUIPC and
immediate-selection muxes on the multiply path. Preserve the normal
a/b inputs for all other ALU operations and the iterative divider.
Add dedicated multiply-operand inputs to alu and wire them internally
from ex_stage; no top-level IO or pipeline stage changes are required.

For the shared product, form signed 33-bit operands
{signed_a && mul_a[31], mul_a} and {signed_b && mul_b[31], mul_b}.
Set signed_a only for MULH/MULHSU and signed_b only for MULH. Assign the
multiply to an explicitly signed 66-bit result. A zero prefix represents
all unsigned 32-bit values as positive; a sign prefix represents each
signed 32-bit value exactly. MUL uses bits 31:0, independent of signedness;
MULH, MULHU and MULHSU use bits 63:32 with their respective sign modes.
Share the identical high-half output arm. Do not apply a post-product
sign correction, absolute-value normalization, partial-product adder
network, new pipeline register or blocking multiply latency.

Preserve all four RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS constants and arithmetic formulas;
their multiplication substitutes must use the same dedicated forwarded
register operands as real multiplication. For every valid decoded multiply
these equal the old a/b values, so routing and retirement semantics remain
identical. Keep DIV/REM real and abstract implementations, their request
and result handshakes, capture metadata and backpressure behavior intact.
Keep nret=1, all decoder legality/trap checks, alignment behavior, bus
handshakes, predictor policy and channel-0 RVFI ordering unchanged.

An isolated implementation of precisely this proposal reached 54.842 MHz
with Gowin placement option 0, versus the reproduced 49.053 MHz champion:
11.8 percent faster for that option. Worst arrival fell from 25.681 to
23.529 ns, DSP resources fell from six to two, and LUTs changed from
2,998 to 3,027 with FFs unchanged at 871. The existing real-arithmetic
ALU and 23-test pipeline cocotb suites passed, including 41,296 extra
multiply checks covering directed chunk/sign boundaries and 10,000
random operand pairs across all four multiplication operations.

The complete isolated vendor probe produced Fmax values 54.842, 55.538
and 55.538 MHz for placement options 0, 1 and 2: median 55.538 MHz,
11.16 percent above the champion median. Stalled CoreMark completed
with start/stop markers at cycles 15,150 and 4,212,597, giving exactly
4,197,447 bracketed cycles, unchanged from the champion. All five
canonical CRCs, the validation UART literal, EBREAK completion and the
absence of out-of-bounds accesses passed the existing evaluator checks.
With ten iterations, the measured probe implies fitness approximately
132.31, above the 124.50538 acceptance threshold. Selftest full-trace
cosim passed with and without imem/dmem stalls. Both real and ALTOPS
elaboration remain required; ALTOPS lint passed in the isolated probe.
The formal proof suite has not been run for this proposal and remains
an implementation gate. These are prototype measurements, not an
orchestrator acceptance result. Preserve the exact operand sizing and
routing when implementing and rebuild with the unchanged evaluation
contract. Remaining forwarding, branch-training and DSP sign-input
paths can limit future gains; do not combine other optimizations here.

implementation_notes:
# Shared signedness-selectable multiplier

Implemented the proposed combinational multiplier datapath in cores/bench
only. alu.sv now has dedicated 32-bit mul_a/mul_b inputs, connected by
ex_stage.sv directly to its existing post-forwarding rs1/rs2 buses.
Ordinary ALU and divider operands retain their original muxes.

Replaced three full-width products with one multiplication of explicitly
signed 33-bit operands into an explicitly signed 66-bit product. The rs1
prefix sign-extends only MULH/MULHSU; the rs2 prefix sign-extends only MULH.
MUL selects bits 31:0. A single shared arm for MULH/MULHU/MULHSU selects
bits 63:32. The four ALTOPS multiplication constants and add/sub formulas
are unchanged and now use the dedicated multiply operands. Divider logic,
handshakes, captured metadata, stage registers, decoder, predictor, bus
interfaces, nret=1 and RVFI channel-0 retirement wiring are unchanged.

Retained all existing ALU and pipeline tests. Added 1,296 exact multiply
checks across 18 directed sign/chunk-boundary operands and 40,000 checks
across 10,000 deterministic random pairs and all four multiply modes.
The random checks deliberately make normal a/b differ from mul_a/mul_b.
Additional checks verify that every ordinary ALU operation and all four
division/remainder operations still use normal a/b.

Pipeline additions cover both source ports through EX/MEM and MEM/WB,
both sources using one writer, younger-writer priority over older matches,
register-file operands, x0, and load-to-multiply dependencies. Multiply
consumers include stores, load/store addresses and taken/untaken branches,
with zero-wait buses and two deterministic stalled runs. Assertions check
exact arithmetic, RVFI source values and memory metadata, contiguous
retirement order, branch successors, and every accepted store transaction.

Local verification:

- Required Verilator lint: PASS, no warnings.
- Verilator lint with RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS: PASS, no warnings.
- Formal: PASS on the initial run, 53 passed / 0 failed. Invoked
  RTL_DIR=cores/bench/rtl CORE_NAME=bench JOBS=8 bash formal/run_all.sh;
  it automatically selected wrapper_si.sv and checks_si.cfg for nret=1.
  No counterexamples and no fix attempts were needed.
- All seven cocotb/pytest unit suites: PASS, including the expanded ALU
  and pipeline suites and the existing EX, IF, decoder, immediate and
  register-file suites.
- NRET=1 make cosim TARGET=bench: PASS. Selftest full-trace comparisons
  passed with and without imem/dmem stalls; stalled CoreMark passed all
  five canonical CRCs and the validation UART literal, reached EBREAK,
  and reported no out-of-bounds accesses.
- Stalled CoreMark markers: start 15,150, stop 4,212,597; exactly
  4,197,447 bracketed cycles, unchanged from the champion.
- make timing TARGET=bench: placement option 0 Fmax 54.254 MHz, worst
  arrival 23.726 ns, two DSP resources.
- NRET=1 make fpga TARGET=bench: placement options 0/1/2 produced
  54.254 / 52.930 / 52.930 MHz, median 52.930 MHz; 2,946 LUT4, 871 FF,
  two DSP resources; reported fitness 126.1 for ten iterations.

No architectural deviations or other optimizations were introduced.
Local timing is below the prototype measurements in the hypothesis but
exceeds the stated acceptance threshold of 124.50538. These are local
checks, not an orchestrator acceptance result. The formal gate uses
ALTOPS; formal-deep real-arithmetic proofs were not run. Real multiplier
arithmetic was checked with the expanded exact Python comparisons and
cosimulation.
lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r3s0 (regression, +5.94%): Sharing RV32M modes through a signed 33x33 product fed directly by forwarded rs1/rs2 bypasses ALU operand muxes and cuts DSPs from six to two, but unchanged CoreMark cycles make the gain depend on final median placement Fmax, which fell from the prototype's 55.538 MHz to 52.930 MHz.

title: Isolate DSP multiplication behind a registered blocking execution unit
motivation:
The champion scores 119.03 at 49.962 MHz and 4,197,447 bracketed cycles.
After removing combinational division and shortening prediction recovery,
Gowin reports a 25.681 ns, 15-cell path from the register file through ID,
EX and the ALU to a data-memory endpoint. The preceding control cleanup
and structural fetch/decode-register attempts exposed the same DSP
multiplication path without improving Fmax. Registering fetch/decode
actually regressed fitness by 10.64 percent. The remaining opportunity
is to split multiply execution itself, so its forwarding, DSP arithmetic
and result selection no longer share one timing interval. CoreMark uses
multiplication in its matrix kernels, so the additional multiply cycles
must be charged against the measured clock gain rather than assumed free.
A fresh placement-option-0 vendor run reproduces the path and explicitly
shows a 3.780 ns DSP multiplier arc after the forwarded-operand muxes.
Architectural tracing of the canonical ELF between the MMIO markers
counts 93,960 MUL instructions and no high-half multiply or divide/rem
instructions; this is instruction-frequency evidence, not a timing or
cycle measurement of the proposed design.

Gowin reports a 25.681 ns, 15-cell path from the register file through ID,
EX and the ALU to a data-memory endpoint. The preceding control cleanup
and structural fetch/decode-register attempts exposed the same DSP
multiplication path without improving Fmax. Registering fetch/decode
actually regressed fitness by 10.64 percent. The remaining opportunity
is to split multiply execution itself, so its forwarding, DSP arithmetic
and result selection no longer share one timing interval. CoreMark uses
multiplication in its matrix kernels, so the additional multiply cycles
must be charged against the measured clock gain rather than assumed free.
A fresh placement-option-0 vendor run reproduces the path and explicitly
shows a 3.780 ns DSP multiplier arc after the forwarded-operand muxes.
Architectural tracing of the canonical ELF between the MMIO markers
counts 93,960 MUL instructions and no high-half multiply or divide/rem
instructions; this is instruction-frequency evidence, not a timing or
cycle measurement of the proposed design.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the combinational MUL, MULH, MULHU and MULHSU paths with one
dedicated registered multiply unit, using a blocking request/completion
protocol analogous to the existing iterative divider. This is one
execution-topology change; keep ordinary integer instructions at their
current latency, the PC-indexed predictor, the combinational fetch/decode
boundary, the divider algorithm, and the nret=1 interface.

Capture the operation and both post-forwarding 32-bit operands on a
valid legal request accepted while EX can advance. Capture the complete
instruction and RVFI source metadata at that same edge. A separate
clocked arithmetic step computes and registers the multiply result from
those captured operands, never directly from live EX forwarding muxes.
Expose the registered result as a stable valid completion until EX/MEM
accepts it. The intended minimum schedule is request/operand capture,
registered product calculation, then completion transfer to EX/MEM:
two additional EX occupancy cycles versus the current fast multiply.
Preserve a real operand-register boundary and a registered arithmetic
result before the ordinary ALU result mux, allowing DSP input/output
register inference while keeping forwarding outside the DSP interval.

A single unsigned 32-by-32 product P is sufficient for all four results.
Register this 64-bit product in the arithmetic step. MUL can complete
directly from its registered low word, with the two extra occupancy
cycles specified above. For high-half operations, add one further
registered selection/correction step before asserting completion, so
the DSP product and high-word subtractors are in separate clock intervals.
MULHU selects P[63:32], MULHSU selects the high
word minus b when a[31] is set, and MULH subtracts b when a[31] is set
and a when b[31] is set, with correction modulo 2^32. Keep multiplication
widths explicit and use DSP-inferable arithmetic. Do not leave a multiply
or high-word correction network in the fast ALU case mux. Completion
reads only stable registered data. This explicitly charges three added
cycles to high-half multiplies without extending ordinary MUL. An
independent fixed-width model of these correction formulas matches exact
signed/unsigned integer multiplication on 100,100 directed/random pairs;
real RTL correctness still requires the existing arithmetic checks.

Hold fetch and ID/EX while multiplication owns EX, drain older EX/MEM
and MEM/WB instructions, and emit invalid side-effect-free EX/MEM bubbles
during the wait. Existing dmem backpressure takes priority and retains
the older request. Do not hold an older store in EX/MEM after it has
completed, repeatedly issue it, or repeatedly retire an older token.
Release ID/EX only when the registered completion is accepted, transfer
its saved metadata exactly once, and retain the completion through dmem
stalls. Reset cancels ownership. Pending multiplication and division
must be mutually exclusive; redirects and predictor updates continue
to occur only for valid advancing instructions. Captured source data
must survive disappearance of older forwarding sources during waits.
Keep channel-0 retirement contiguous and all traps, memory masks and
architectural semantics unchanged.

Retain the exact existing RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS formulas for every MUL
variant and register their results through the same ownership and
completion interface without changing any formal configuration or
weakening real arithmetic tests. Update direct ALU and execute tests
for the new latency rather than dropping their exact-result assertions.

Acceptance requires Fnew/49.962 divided by Cnew/4197447 to exceed 1.046.
Charging two added cycles to each of the traced 93,960 MUL instructions
gives a first-order estimate of 4,385,367 bracketed cycles, a 4.48 percent
increase. At that cycle count the clock must exceed about 54.60 MHz;
a 65 MHz clock would yield about 24.52 percent fitness gain. Bus-stall
overlap and the changed phase of the pseudo-random ready sequence can
alter this estimate, so acceptance uses actual marker cycles and the
vendor median clock, never the architectural frequency estimate.
Predict 20 percent with medium confidence. The key uncertainties are
dynamic multiply frequency and whether register-file, predictor or
divider-step timing becomes the next limit. Validate canonical stalled
CoreMark CRCs and marker cycles, existing formal and cosim gates, exact
RV32M multiply results and Gowin median Fmax. This is an architectural
prediction, not a claim of measured improvement.

title: Predict through load-dependent branches with delayed registered resolution
motivation:
The current champion's 64-entry tagged next-PC predictor already removes
most control-transfer bubbles and scores 119.03 at 49.962 MHz over
4,197,447 bracketed CoreMark cycles. Merely enlarging its table has little
remaining headroom: the previous architectural model found only 62,551
next-PC errors at 64 entries versus 58,167 at 128. A fresh execution of
the canonical RV32IM, -O3, 2K, ten-iteration ELF finds 135,320 immediately
load-dependent conditional branches among 2,922,015 instructions strictly
between the marker stores. The hazard unit currently stalls these
branches even though fetch already knows their predicted successor.
Only 2,830 of those branches have a next-PC error in the existing
immediate-training trace model, making them useful speculative candidates.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Use the existing next-PC prediction to issue legal conditional branches
immediately behind a producer load without the usual load-use bubble.
Resolve only these dependent branches one stage later, from a registered
load result, while continuing fetch along their captured prediction.
Keep ordinary branches, jumps and all other load consumers on their
existing paths. This is one predictor-enabled speculative branch policy,
Keep the existing 64-entry target/direction table and combinational IF/ID
boundary. The architectural change is how the predictor is used to let
dependent branches issue before their operands become available.

At decode, validate the BRANCH opcode and funct3 before exempting an
actual rs1/rs2 dependence on a valid, legal, aligned, nonzero-destination
EX load. Expose a narrow producer-eligibility signal from EX; determine
load alignment with the forwarded base plus immediate low two bits,
rather than feeding the full ALU-result mux into hazard control. A
misaligned producer retains the existing load-use stall and trap behavior.
In EX identify the branch's matching producer in the existing EX/MEM
register; attach explicit deferred-resolution metadata to EX/MEM only.
This avoids adding decode-stage speculation metadata or changing ID/EX.
Capture the branch PC,
prediction, target, operation, both forwarded operands and which source
operands need the immediately preceding load. Do not resolve or train
that branch using the load's effective address as operand data. When the
branch reaches MEM, substitute the preceding load's registered WB result
for each marked source, resolve the real branch condition and alignment
trap, and produce the architectural RVFI operands and successor. No
combinational dmem-data-to-EX comparison or ALU bypass is introduced.
Suppress EX branch redirects, predictor training and operand-dependent
alignment traps for deferred branches. Compute their actual trap in MEM
after both operands are correct; never carry a trap inferred from the
producer load's effective address. Compute target and sequential-successor
prediction comparisons in parallel, as in the champion's recovery path.

Correct predictions leave the speculative younger instruction in EX
advancing normally. An older delayed-branch mismatch overrides a younger
EX redirect, kills the younger EX/MEM transfer and ID/EX instruction,
prevents wrong-path stores, register writes, divider requests and
predictor updates, and recovers fetch even when imemReady is low. Its
recovery must override a younger divider wait; a divider must not accept
a wrong-path request on that edge. Preserve older WB retirement. Train
each delayed branch once from its real MEM outcome; arbitrate simultaneous
younger EX feedback with older MEM feedback taking priority, never train
an unresolved dependent branch, and safely drop younger training if the
single predictor write port is occupied. Lost training affects prediction
quality only. Dmem holds preserve the dependent branch until the producer
load completes; retain any non-load forwarded operand across those holds.
Keep recovery off instruction data, wide register payload enables and
wide payload clears. Kill younger validity and side-effect controls only;
invalid tokens must neither forward stale writers nor issue memory work.
An older MEM recovery must flush ID/EX even when its younger instruction
requests a load-use or divider hold. The resolving branch must advance to
WB and train exactly once independently of a younger divider's EX wait.

The opportunity is 135,320 architectural load-to-branch pairs, not a
measured RTL cycle reduction. A standalone trace-driven scheduling model
with the same xorshift32 bus-ready policy, pre-edge predictor lookup,
EX training and single-port older-first deferred training estimates
4,197,329 cycles for the champion policy and 4,063,352 for this policy
with seed 0xDEADBEEF. The former is close to the recorded 4,197,447;
these model runs start at the timing window with empty pipeline/table
state, so they are not exact reproductions of the evaluation's initial
predictor state or random phase and do not establish RTL correctness.
Across four seeds the model suggests about 3.2--3.3 percent higher
iterations/cycle, not a five-percent cycle gain. Delayed recovery costs
an extra younger slot; fetch stalls hide some load-use bubbles, while
removing a ready-cycle bubble also avoids the subsequent fetch retry.
Model comparisons with one-, two-, four- and eight-entry predicted fetch
queues show diminishing returns and require a deeper recovery pipeline;
the targeted deferred-branch policy keeps the champion frontend intact.

The five-percent fitness estimate is deliberately low confidence: at
4,063,352 cycles the vendor median Fmax must exceed about 50.60 MHz
to beat 119.03 by 4.6 percent, versus 49.962 MHz today. The model's cycle
saving alone does not meet acceptance. No Fmax improvement is measured
or guaranteed, and the added MEM comparator/kill routing may reduce it.
This predictor slot targets a much larger remaining cycle opportunity
than table enlargement while requiring only about 1.3 percent additional
Fmax for acceptance; keep recovery narrow to minimize that timing risk.
Keep nret=1, decoder
legality, arithmetic, all memory/RVFI invariants and the evaluation files
unchanged. Validate stalled CoreMark CRCs, marker cycles, formal/cosim
correctness and Gowin timing before accepting this low-confidence gain.

title: Register predictor training feedback before the table write
motivation:
Registering the blocking multiplier raised the champion to 129.51 fitness
at 56.790 MHz over 4,384,920 bracketed CoreMark cycles. Its reported worst
Gowin path now runs from cpu/u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s0 through ID and EX to
cpu/u_if/tags_tags_0_0_s: 22.917 ns arrival across 36 cells. Predictor
training still feeds live EX advancement, target alignment and outcome
directly into asynchronous tag lookup, counter update and table write
logic. Registering that feedback is a local opportunity to split the
remaining control path without adding an instruction pipeline stage.
Prior micro_opt attempts removed redirect fanout or shared combinational
multiplication; neither isolated predictor table maintenance. The
failed registered fetch boundary and delayed load-branch experiment
argue for preserving immediate recovery and the present issue pipeline.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Insert one unconditional register boundary on the predictor_update_t
feedback inside if_stage, immediately before all predictor table update
bookkeeping. EX continues to generate exactly its existing update and
redirect signals. Capture the update payload every nonreset clock,
independently of fetch acceptance, stalls or update.valid; capture its
valid bit every clock and clear that bit on reset. Payload registers
need no reset. The table consumes the previous cycle's registered update,
never the live EX feedback. This stage accepts one update each cycle and
applies it once on the following edge; it must neither hold and replay a
valid update nor suppress a pending update because fetch or EX is now
stalled. Reset cancels the pending update and clears table validity.

Derive update_index, update tag comparison, matching-entry invalidation,
target/tag/unconditional writes and saturating counter decisions solely
from the registered feedback and current table contents. Compute the
update hit when applying the update, rather than registering a hit from
its capture cycle: consecutive allocations and invalidations at the
same index must observe the preceding committed update. Retain all 64
entries, full PC tags, target widths, two-bit direction counters,
initial counter states, and matching-only noncontrol invalidation.
Preserve asynchronous PC-only prediction and synchronous RAM writes,
with no training bypass into lookup and no payload-memory resets.

Keep redirect and redirect_target on their current immediate EX-to-PC
path, with recovery overriding imem stalls. Preserve the combinational
fetch/decode boundary, captured predicted_next_pc, ordinary instruction
latency, all hazard and memory handshake priorities, and registered
blocking MUL/DIV behavior. The only behavioral difference is that table
learning becomes visible one cycle later; a stale prediction is still
corrected by the existing successor comparisons and validity/control
kills. This is a feedback-retiming micro-optimization, with no new
prediction policy or speculative instruction execution rule.

The prediction is that splitting live EX resolution from RAM update
control raises median Gowin Fmax enough to outweigh a small training
freshness penalty. Expected fitness improvement is 12 percent with
medium confidence; neither a clock gain nor unchanged cycles is yet
measured. With unchanged cycles, acceptance requires Fmax greater than
59.403 MHz; in general Fnew/56.790 divided by Cnew/4384920 must exceed
1.046. Immediate redirect, ordinary ALU and divider recurrence paths may
become the next timing limit. Very short loops or changing JALR targets
may add prediction misses, so evaluate actual canonical stalled CoreMark
marker cycles, CRCs and median vendor Fmax rather than assuming zero cost.
Preserve nret=1, exact RVFI operands/order/traps, decoder legality, every
arithmetic check, and all immutable evaluation files.

implementation_notes:
# Predictor feedback register

Implemented the hypothesis in `cores/bench/rtl/if_stage.sv`. A `predictor_update_t`
register captures every payload field on every nonreset edge, including
invalid bubbles and cycles with fetch or execution backpressure. Its valid
bit captures every cycle and resets independently. Table maintenance uses
only the previous cycle's registered feedback. The update hit is computed
from the current table when the queued update is applied, so consecutive
allocations, counter updates and matching invalidations observe committed
state. Reset clears pending validity and all table validity.

The 64-entry table, full tags, target widths, counter initialization and
saturation, matching-only invalidation, asynchronous prediction and
synchronous payload writes retain their existing behavior. Payload memories
and feedback payload registers have no reset assignment. EX feedback,
immediate redirect priority, fetch/decode boundary, hazard priorities,
blocking MUL/DIV, RVFI and nret=1 were not changed. There are no architectural
deviations from the proposed implementation.

`cores/bench/test/test_if_stage.py` retains the original checks with the extra training
edge and adds consecutive same-index feedback, application-time hits,
bubbles without replay, unconditional payload capture, reset cancellation,
stalls and redirects, all 64 entries, and randomized queued-table checks.
`cores/bench/test/test_pipeline.py` adds a one-update queue reference table to the
existing monitor and checks every observed prediction, captured prediction
and immediate recovery/hold transition. A single-instruction self-loop test
checks the two delayed cold corrections, subsequent matching invalidation,
prolonged bus holds, retirement operands/PCs/order and exactly one accepted
store. The only existing prediction expectation changed is the collided
transfer's recovery sequence: its prior tag remains visible until the
source's queued allocation commits. Existing architectural, arithmetic,
trap, memory-effect and ISS comparison assertions remain intact.

Local validation:

- Required Verilator lint command: pass, no warnings.
- `RTL_DIR=cores/bench/rtl CORE_NAME=bench JOBS=8 bash formal/run_all.sh`:
  pass on the first RTL attempt, 53 passed / 0 failed; no counterexamples
  and no formal fix attempts.
- `make test TARGET=bench`: all 7 unit-test runners passed, including the
  arithmetic checks, 6 fetch-stage tests and 28 pipeline tests.
- `NRET=1 make cosim TARGET=bench`: pass, selftest RVFI comparison both
  without stalls and with random imem/dmem stalls, plus canonical stalled
  CoreMark CRC validation. The unqualified Makefile invocation initially
  compiled the immutable harness with its NRET=2 default; setting the build
  environment to the core's declared NRET=1 resolved that harness mismatch.
- Canonical `run_coremark_ipc` check: completed, 10 iterations, bracketed
  marker cycles = 4,384,920. All five canonical CRCs and the validation
  message passed the unchanged evaluator.
- `make timing TARGET=bench` and the same Gowin evaluator with
  `--all-options`: all placements completed. Fmax options 0/1/2 were
  54.467 / 56.156 / 56.156 MHz; median = 56.156 MHz. Option 0 reports
  3,319 logic cells, 1,045 registers, 8 LUT-RAMs, 9 BSRAMs and 2 DSPs.
- `git diff --check`: pass. Tracked changes are limited to the three
  permitted RTL/test files. This notes file is at the worktree root as
  requested by instruction 5 and read by the orchestrator's `_read_notes`.

Performance concern: the measured hypothesis does not meet acceptance.
Cycles are unchanged from 4,384,920, but median Fmax decreased from 56.790
to 56.156 MHz. Measured fitness is 128.06619 iterations/second; the relative
fitness ratio is 0.988836, below the required 1.046 (59.403 MHz with these
cycles). Option 0's worst path is now register-file through ID/EX/ALU to
dmem, with 23.654 ns arrival across 16 cells. Long remaining predictor
paths end at B-port read addresses (`ADB`), consistent with the preserved
immediate recovery/fetch-address path. The feedback retiming remains in
place for the orchestrator's independent evaluation; no unrelated timing
or prediction-policy changes were attempted.

title: Split operand forwarding from execution with a registered operand stage
motivation:
The champion scores 129.51 iterations/second at median Gowin Fmax
56.790 MHz over 4,384,920 bracketed CoreMark cycles. Registered blocking
multiply and divide removed the earlier arithmetic limits. A fresh
make timing TARGET=bench on the unchanged champion reproduces placement
option 0 at 56.745 MHz and exposes two nearly tied bottlenecks: the
22.917 ns register-file-to-predictor path and a 22.906 ns WB destination
comparison/forwarding-to-ALU-to-dmem path. Other register-file-to-dmem
paths are 22.892 ns. Optimizing just predictor feedback would leave
the memory-side paths limiting the clock.

The detailed report shows BRAM register-file clock-to-output followed
by ID bypass, EX forwarding/operand muxes and execution, all in one
clock interval. The worst WB path carries a forwarding-select change
through operand selection, the ALU and its result mux into dmem.
The earlier structural IF/ID-register attempt lost 10.64 percent
because it added fetch latency while the execution path remained
critical. The successful registered-multiplier lesson is to put the
boundary inside the actual arithmetic/operand path. This proposal
applies that separation to ordinary execution and branch resolution.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add an operand-preparation stage between the existing decoded ID/EX
payload and execution. The pipeline becomes fetch/decode, operand
preparation, execute, memory, writeback. Register the fully selected
and forwarded rs1/rs2 values, ALU a/b operands, instruction controls
and retirement metadata in an O/X bundle. Also prepare and register
PC+4 and PC-relative target in this bundle. The fast ALU, comparisons
and JALR addition must consume these registers exclusively, with no
live register-file or forwarding mux feeding execution. Keep the
existing combinational IF/ID, 64-entry predictor and registered
blocking M arithmetic. This is a single structural split of operand
selection from execution, not a new fetch stage or predictor policy.

Preserve one-instruction-per-cycle steady-state issue, including
adjacent dependent ordinary ALU instructions. For each source in O,
select the youngest older writer: the instruction executing in X,
then registered EX/MEM, then WB, then the saved register-file value.
Add a same-cycle X-result-to-O-register bypass for a valid fast result
or accepted completed M result. It is permitted to end at the O/X
operand register; it must never feed a same-cycle execute input.
Thus adjacent ALU consumers need no additional RAW bubble and the
feedback path starts at registered X operands. The producer's live
result and consumer's forwarded operands cannot form a combinational
loop. Qualify forwarding by actual architectural write permission,
including x0, illegal encodings and alignment-trapped jumps.

An unresolved youngest load or M producer blocks a dependent O token;
never fall through to an older same-register writer or forward a
load's effective address as its value. Use registered WB load data,
avoiding a new combinational dmem-data-to-execute bypass. This
conservatively adds one bubble to immediate load consumers versus
the current one-bubble policy. When O waits on such a load, hold O
and fetch/decode while injecting an invalid X token so older work
drains. Reassess readiness until the correct load result is available.
Determine dependencies from actual legal source use so instruction
immediate bits are not treated as unavailable register operands.
Alignment-trapped loads must leave the old architectural rd value
visible to later consumers. A blocked consumer must retain values
already supplied by an older writer even after forwarding sources
drain: snoop accepted WB writes into matching held O source fields,
or retain resolved source values with explicit pending-source bits.
Include both-source and same-rd-younger-writer cases.

Keep MUL/DIV requests and ownership in X, using its registered operands.
Start each valid legal operation once, hold X until completion, and
allow older MEM/WB work to drain. Hold younger O and fetch/decode when
X cannot accept them; completion may bypass its registered result to
the waiting O consumer on the acceptance edge. Keep the current real
arithmetic, high-word corrections and exact ALTOPS formulas unchanged.
Older dmem backpressure freezes EX/MEM, X and O, retains stable memory
outputs, and permits only the existing once-only WB drain. Preserve
retained WB forwarding data even after its retirement valid clears.
Distinguish a blocked O consumer from a blocked X owner: the former
bubbles X when it can drain; the latter holds X and bubbles EX/MEM.

Resolve and train branches in X from registered operands and the
captured prediction. Keep current parallel successor comparisons.
On an advancing mismatch, redirect fetch with the existing priority
over imem stalls and squash both younger O/X input and decoded O
tokens, including their side-effect controls. Preserve the resolving
instruction's transfer into EX/MEM and older retirement. Never launch
a wrong-path M request, memory access or writer; invalid tokens cannot
redirect or train. Recovery costs one additional younger slot only
on next-PC errors; correctly predicted branches keep streaming.
Train each advancing instruction exactly once and reset every new
valid/ownership bit. Keep recovery off raw instruction data and wide
payload clears. Maintain exact captured RVFI operands and contiguous
channel-0 retirement order with the unchanged nret=1 interface.

Historical tracing found 135,320 immediate load-to-branch pairs and
about 62,551 next-PC errors in the same CoreMark instruction stream.
Those are model counts, not measured penalties for this champion;
other load consumers, false dependencies, bus overlap and altered
training latency also affect cycles. Use six percent more bracketed
cycles, about 4,648,015, as a provisional engineering budget. At that
count, beating the champion by 4.6 percent requires median Fmax above
62.97 MHz. A 70 MHz result would score about 150.60 iterations/second,
a 16.28 percent gain. Predict a 16 percent fitness improvement with
medium confidence. The main risks are the X-result-to-O bypass becoming
the next timing limit, extra load stalls exceeding the budget, and
placement cost of the new registers. The actual hypothesis succeeds
only if (new_Fmax / 56.790) / (new_cycles / 4384920) exceeds 1.046.
Preserve all decoder defaults, traps, arithmetic, memory bounds,
canonical CRCs, marker timing and unchanged formal/cosim/eval gates.

title: Predictor-guided fall-through fetch skid buffer
motivation:
The champion scores 129.51 at 56.790 MHz over 4,384,920 bracketed
CoreMark cycles. Its existing 64-entry tagged predictor already removes
most taken-transfer bubbles. Earlier predictor work found little gain
from more entries; delayed load-dependent branch resolution saved 3.17
percent of cycles but missed acceptance after its timing loss.
The current frontend nevertheless stops fetching throughout load-use,
dmem and blocking MUL/DIV holds, throwing away available instruction-bus
cycles. Approximately 22 percent random instruction-bus stalls then
create bubbles after those holds finish. Registered multiplication has
added useful fetch-ahead opportunities compared with the earlier core.

Temporary vendor experiments on this exact champion reproduced its
56.790 MHz median. Delayed predictor training gave 54.678 MHz, forced
distributed predictor storage gave 57.071 MHz, and precomputed direct
prediction-match flags gave 51.604 MHz, all with unchanged CoreMark
cycles. Moving all control recovery to MEM reached only 57.693 MHz.
These results expose an ALU timing ceiling and do not justify a timing-
only predictor change. A predictor-guided fetch buffer instead seeks
meaningful cycle savings while preserving the common empty-buffer path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one elastic, fall-through fetch skid entry inside if_stage, holding
the complete if_id_t token: instruction, its PC, its exact predicted
successor and validity. Keep the current 64-entry predictor algorithm,
immediate EX resolution and single-retirement pipeline. While ID is
held and the entry is empty, accept an imemReady instruction, save the
token and advance the fetch PC along its captured prediction. Fetch
thereby uses otherwise discarded ready cycles during load-use, dmem
and registered arithmetic holds. When the entry is full, offer its
token to ID independently of the current instruction-bus readiness.

Use combinational bypass when the entry is empty: out is the raw
current fetch token and acceptance can go straight to ID without an
added pipeline cycle. When the buffered head is consumed, simultaneously
replace it with the current ready fetch if available; otherwise clear
its valid bit. When a full entry cannot drain, hold the fetch address,
entry and its prediction stable. Accept no instruction twice. Predictor
lookup continues to use only the registered fetch PC. Store the exact
predicted_next_pc used when fetch advances; never recompute a queued
instruction's prediction after subsequent table updates.

Distinguish raw io_imemReady from availability of the token presented to
ID. Feed the hazard unit's existing imem_ready input from if_id_w.valid,
so an occupied buffer can issue while the external bus stalls and
load-use checks inspect the actual offered head's source fields.
Preserve dmem/ex_wait/load-use hold and bubble priorities. Treat the
existing if_stage stall input as backpressure on the offered ID token;
derive fetch acceptance locally from raw imem_ready and entry capacity,
including simultaneous dequeue/enqueue. A missing head still bubbles
ID as before. No combinational dmem-result bypass or hazard exemption
is introduced. Do not change arithmetic or the pipeline stages.

Recovery has highest priority: invalidate the queued younger token and
discard any same-edge fetch, update fetch PC to redirect_target even
with an unavailable bus or a full entry, and retain the existing narrow
ID validity/side-effect kill. Correct predictions leave queued work
intact. A wrong prediction can now have one additional younger fetch
in the entry, but neither that entry nor the current raw fetch may
create a wrong-path memory request or retirement. Reset clears queue
validity and restores RESET_PC; stale payload need not be reset.
A held EX instruction still trains only once when it advances, and
buffered tokens must preserve order through imem/dmem stalls and
blocking arithmetic completion.

Expect approximately six percent higher fitness from fewer fetch
bubbles, with low confidence until measured. At unchanged Fmax, beating
the 4.6 percent acceptance threshold requires fewer than approximately
4,192,084 bracketed cycles, a saving of roughly 193,000 cycles. Six
percent improvement corresponds to approximately 4,136,717 cycles.
These are break-even calculations, not measured buffer results.
The token-selection mux may lower Fmax and a one-entry buffer may hide
too few stalls; measure vendor median timing and actual marker cycles
together. Preserve canonical CRCs, memory bounds, decoder legality,
nret=1 and all RVFI invariants. Run unchanged formal/cosim/CoreMark
gates. This hypothesis changes predictor-guided fetch scheduling only;
do not combine it with the rejected training, storage or recovery trials.

title: Banked distributed-RAM register file with reset validity
motivation:
The champion scores 137.70 at 56.873 MHz over 4,130,235 bracketed
CoreMark cycles. Its worst reported Gowin path begins at the register
file's inferred block RAM and reaches predictor storage through ID
and EX in 22.713 ns. Earlier micro_opt changes to redirect fanout,
multiplier sharing and registered predictor training did not exceed
the acceptance threshold; training isolation also exposed another
register-file-to-ALU-to-memory path. Register-file access is therefore
a common starting point worth shortening without adding pipeline
stages or changing instruction throughput. The current 32x32 array
resets every payload word and leaves its physical memory mapping to
synthesis. No logged micro_opt attempt directly changes that mapping.

hypothesis.motivation:
The champion scores 137.70 at 56.873 MHz over 4,130,235 bracketed
CoreMark cycles. Its worst reported Gowin path begins at the register
file's inferred block RAM and reaches predictor storage through ID
and EX in 22.713 ns. Earlier micro_opt changes to redirect fanout,
multiplier sharing and registered predictor training did not exceed
the acceptance threshold; training isolation also exposed another
register-file-to-ALU-to-memory path. Register-file access is therefore
a common starting point worth shortening without adding pipeline
stages or changing instruction throughput. The current 32x32 array
resets every payload word and leaves its physical memory mapping to
synthesis. No logged micro_opt attempt directly changes that mapping.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Apply one local register-file implementation optimization: implement
both asynchronous read ports using independent, coherent copies of
two 16x32 distributed-RAM banks, instead of the inferred block-RAM
register file. Both copies receive the same accepted nonzero write.
Use address bit 4 to select the bank and bits 3:0 to index each bank.
Express each bank as an asynchronous-read, synchronous-write memory,
with (* syn_ramstyle = "distributed_ram" *) on each array. This is the
supported value in GowinSynthesis SUG550 section 5.15; "distributed"
is not a valid value. Keep the RTL portable for Verilator and
riscv-formal; do not instantiate vendor
primitives or alter FPGA tool options or wrappers. Inspect synthesis
reports to confirm that the register-file payload maps to RAM16
resources rather than BSRAM. Banking and read-port replication are
part of this single physical implementation change, not new stages.

Remove reset from the RAM payload write processes. Preserve the exact
architectural reset behavior with a 32-bit written/valid bitmap:
synchronous reset clears all bits; an accepted nonzero write sets its
bit. Each read returns zero for x0 or an unwritten register, regardless
of stale or uninitialized payload data. Reset also suppresses payload
writes, including a concurrent w_en. Retain existing combinational
write-first priority: x0 returns zero first, then a matching enabled
nonzero write returns w_data, then a valid stored register returns its
bank output, otherwise zero. In particular, an enabled matching write
must bypass even before the valid bit has been set. Preserve the
current combinational behavior during reset and synchronous clearing
at the reset edge. Mid-program reset must hide every old stored value.

Keep the module's existing ports, two zero-cycle read ports, one
positive-edge write port, register values and pipeline timing intact.
The hypothesis predicts a shorter common operand-access path and
unchanged stalled CoreMark marker cycles. Its principal risk is that
duplicated RAM and validity/bank selection cost more routing than the
block-RAM access saves, or another critical path takes over. Do not
combine this with ALU, forwarding, predictor or pipeline changes.
At unchanged cycles, the champion's 4.6 percent acceptance threshold
requires median Fmax above 59.489158 MHz and fitness above 144.0342.
An isolated prototype reproduced champion placement option 0 at
57.412 MHz and obtained 59.722, 59.778 and 59.778 MHz with the banked
file: median 59.778 MHz, 5.108 percent above the champion's scored
median. The prototype mapped to 32 RAM16 resources and seven total
BSRAMs, versus eight RAM16 resources and nine BSRAMs before, at 3,513
LUT4 and 1,052 FF. Its worst path moved from RF-originating feedback
to forwarding/ALU paths. These results support the proposed physical
mechanism but leave only a small margin over the acceptance threshold.

The prototype used bank1_lo, bank1_hi, bank2_lo and bank2_hi as four
logic [31:0] arrays [0:15], written_q as the 32-bit validity vector,
and stored1/stored2 as the two bank-selected payload buses. Define
write_accept = !reset && w_en && w_addr != 0. One clocked process
clears written_q on reset or sets written_q[w_addr] on write_accept;
another process writes both matching low-bank copies when
write_accept && !w_addr[4], or both high-bank copies when
write_accept && w_addr[4]. Reads select high/low payload using bit 4
before the existing x0, write-first and written-bit qualification.
Reproduce this simple inferred-memory structure during implementation.

Canonical stalled CoreMark completed at the exact champion marker
count of 4,130,235 cycles, with EBREAK, all five canonical CRCs,
the validation UART literal and no out-of-bounds access. This implies
prototype fitness 144.7327 for ten iterations, above 144.0342. The
existing five register-file tests, an additional 1,600-cycle random
scoreboard including repeated resets and simultaneous read/write
bypass, and all 31 pipeline tests passed. Full RVFI trace comparisons
passed for selftest/random1/random2/random3 with and without bus
stalls. The supported distributed_ram attribute reproduced all three
timing results above without an invalid-attribute warning. Full
riscv-formal has not been run for this
prototype and remains an implementation gate. Rebuild median timing
and CoreMark with the unchanged evaluator before claiming acceptance;
these measurements are research probes, not an orchestrator result.

Preserve nret=1, all decoder/trap checks, memory handshake semantics,
RV32M arithmetic and every RVFI retirement invariant. Retain existing
register-file tests and add write/read sweeps across both banks and
both ports, same-address bypass on both ports, simultaneous writes
and unrelated reads, x0 writes, and a second reset after filling the
array. Run existing pipeline/formal/cosim gates and verify canonical
CoreMark CRCs, validation UART text and bounded memory accesses.

motivation:
The champion reaches 137.70 CoreMark iterations/second at median Gowin
Fmax 56.873 MHz and 4,130,235 bracketed cycles. A fresh unchanged-core

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the inferred memory register file with 31 independently
enabled 32-bit fabric flip-flop words and two combinational, explicitly
decoded read networks. Use constant-index generated words, not a
dynamically indexed writable/readable memory array. Decode each read
address to one-hot word selects, form masked word contributions, and
combine them in a complete balanced binary OR tree with 32 leaves
and five reduction levels; the x0 leaf is constant zero. Instantiate
each nonzero word's clocked process inside its own generate block,
using a constant five-bit local address for write and read comparisons.
Each process resets its word to zero or writes w_data when w_en and
w_addr match. The read-port priority remains x0, then matching live WB
write data, then the tree result. This structure must synthesize as fabric registers,
not BSRAM or distributed memory. Do not instantiate vendor primitives
that would bypass the existing formal toolchain.

x0 hardwiring, one synchronous write port and both write-first bypasses
exactly. The two read networks terminate at the existing ID/EX rs1_val
and rs2_val flip-flops. Keep those registers and their current hold and
flush semantics intact; execution must still read registered operands
plus its existing EX/MEM and MEM/WB forwarding paths. Removing RAM
inference prevents synthesis from absorbing the operand capture into

title: Backward-branch loop stream predictor with instruction replay
motivation:
The champion's 64-entry next-PC predictor already removes most transfer
bubbles. Prior trace data shows little headroom from a larger BTB.
Additional predicted fetch buffering also has diminishing returns:
isolated four- and eight-entry prototypes measured 4,032,232 and
4,029,095 cycles versus the champion's 4,130,235, only about 2.5 percent
gain at unchanged Fmax. Instead, recognize repeated short loops from
resolved backward branches and replay their previously fetched words
during instruction-bus stalls.

A 64-word loop prototype with registered discovery and FENCE.I recovery
measured 3,919,730 bracketed cycles, 5.37 percent higher iterations/cycle.
All canonical CRCs passed, EBREAK completed and no OOB access occurred.
Its placement-option-0 Fmax was 54.419 MHz; this prototype does not
demonstrate acceptance. The proposed implementation must preserve the
cycle saving while minimizing replay lookup and validity fanout.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one branch-discovered loop stream predictor to if_stage, retaining
the champion's existing BTB, immediate EX resolution and one-entry
fall-through skid buffer. A valid, advancing, legal, aligned, taken
conditional backward branch identifies a replay region from its target
through its branch PC, inclusive. Accept only regions of at most 64
aligned instruction words: branch PC minus target at most 252 bytes.
Track one region with full 32-bit base/end PCs, region validity and
64 per-word fill-valid bits. Allocate only branch-discovered loop regions.

Register a separate copy of EX feedback for loop discovery only.
Capture payload each clock and clear validity on reset; consume each
valid update once on the following edge. Compute backward direction,
span and descriptor replacement from that registered copy. Keep
original BTB training and immediate EX recovery unchanged. Changing
the descriptor invalidates every replay slot; repeated resolution of
the same loop retains filled slots. Never hold and replay a valid
discovery update during fetch or execution stalls.

Fill an unreset 64-by-32 instruction array only from real accepted
imemReady responses whose full fetch PC lies inside the current region.
Index slots by PC[7:2]. A contiguous region of at most 64 words has no
repeated index, including across a 256-byte boundary. Reset validity
only. Use distributed asynchronous-read storage for this small replay
array to avoid adding another predictor-side BSRAM address endpoint;
do not alter the existing BTB storage or arithmetic. Keep the common
ready-bus data path shallow, and keep discovery off payload enables.
Descriptor replacement clears slot validity even with a simultaneous
old-region fill; payload written on that edge must remain invalid.

Prefer a current ready bus response over saved instruction data and
refresh its slot. When imemReady is low, an in-range filled slot can
supply the offered instruction. Otherwise preserve stalled fetch.
Internal availability is imemReady OR replay-hit. Replay acceptance
is not an accepted external response and must not fill a slot.
Every accepted internal token retains its full PC, instruction and
exact BTB-predicted successor in the existing skid buffer. Advance
fetch PC once per accepted token, respect skid capacity, and continue
using offered-token validity for hazard checks.

EX still validates every control transfer from real forwarded operands.
Misprediction recovery overrides stalls and discards queued and
same-edge younger tokens. Loop predictions never bypass operand checks,
target alignment, memory side-effect discipline or retirement. Ordinary
recovery may retain immutable loop payloads, because every replay use
is guarded by the full region and slot validity.

Add an advancing FENCE.I indication to predictor feedback. For a legal
opcode 0x0f/funct3=1 instruction, invalidate the replay region and all
slots, cancel pending loop discovery, and force immediate recovery to
PC+4 so younger prefetched instructions are refetched. Invalidation
takes priority over discovery and fills, including a previous branch's
registered discovery. Reset likewise cancels pending discovery and all
replay validity. Preserve existing decoder legality and architectural
FENCE/FENCE.I NOP results. Changed instruction memory followed by
FENCE.I must never expose a stale queued or replayed instruction.

Expect five percent fitness improvement with low confidence. At
3,919,730 cycles, acceptance above 137.70 times 1.046 requires median
Fmax above approximately 56.458 MHz. The registered prototype's
54.419 MHz option-0 result exposes a real timing risk; distributed
replay storage is an unmeasured refinement, not evidence of a win.
Measure actual revised marker cycles and all three vendor placement
options. Run unchanged formal/cosim/CRC gates. Preserve nret=1, all
decoder/trap/memory/RVFI invariants, arithmetic and evaluation files.
